meta.notes: Layer 1 experiments. Scenarios come from data/scenarios/; every other cell is a dataclass override of campus_rush or baseline_flat. Cells whose estimated peak load exceeds 0.95 use 60 replicates, the rest use 100 (first seed 0, stride 1). Paired differences use common random numbers on identical seeds. Variability and patience cells use a two-segment unit demand profile so the fixed-service cell also runs on the event-driven dispatch path (a single flat segment would silently use the baseline path and confound the comparison). The balk decision compares the customer's threshold with the engine's wait estimate divided by the number of staff units ON SHIFT at the arrival instant; these cells have no shift windows, so it equals the worker count, but the library scenarios with late shift starts and breaks are not credited with absent staff.

peak_factor.definition: multiplier_i(f) = multiplier_i ** f, daily mean rescaled back to the quoted rate

peak_vs_flat.note: Same daily mean demand. The peak profile raises the peak-hour busy ratio and the p95 wait while the daily utilisation actually falls, because abandonment removes work from the system.

peak_factor_scan.note: Daily mean demand is held fixed; the multiplier shape is raised to multiplier**factor. J-shaped cost of peakiness: p95, balking and profit move even though the daily mean is unchanged.

variability.note: Make-time variability moves the upper tail much more than the mean: the p95 ratio at CV 0.75 versus deterministic grows with load while the mean wait moves only a little.

patience.note: With arrival-time balking active, reneging almost never binds: the balk threshold decides who leaves. The balk decision compares the customer's threshold with the engine's wait estimate divided by the number of staff units on shift at that instant (these cells have no shift windows, so that is the worker count). The reneging-only table isolates reneging by switching balking off.

batch.note: At a fixed arrival-event rate a higher batch probability is mostly a demand increase; holding the daily customer mean fixed isolates the burstiness effect, which is smaller but still negative for profit.
